item.title: GDOL extends In-School Youth Program application deadline to Oct. 30
item.description: The Guam Department of Labor and Guam Community College have extended the application deadline for the In-School Youth Year-Round Program to Oct. 30, following disruptions caused by Typhoon Champi. The previous deadline was Oct. 24. The extension gives students and families additional time to complete and submit applications.
item.content:encoded:
The Guam Department of Labor and Guam Community College have extended the application deadline for the In-School Youth Year-Round Program to Oct. 30, following disruptions caused by Typhoon Champi.

The previous deadline was Oct. 24. The extension gives students and families additional time to complete and submit applications.

The program offers eligible 11th-grade students professional development, communications, customer service, and leadership training, along with paid employment opportunities. It has also expanded to include students enrolled in GCC’s Career and Technical Education program.

Participants take part in a two-week winter session and a one-week spring session before completing six weeks of paid summer employment with private-sector employers in fields or industries that interest them. All sessions provide a stipend.

To qualify, students must be in the 11th grade or be part of the GCC Career and Technical Education program and meet other program eligibility requirements.

Interested students can apply online at bit.ly/inschoolyouth or contact their school counselor for more information.

For assistance, contact the American Job Center at 671-475-7500 or email ajc.training@dol.guam.gov . Additional information about the department’s youth program is available at dol.guam.gov .

item.title: Breaking Wave Theatre redirects show proceeds to Typhoon Champi recovery
item.description: Breaking Wave Theatre Company is redirecting proceeds from its upcoming live tabletop adventure show to support local recovery efforts following Typhoon Champi. The nonprofit will host “Tides of Fantasy: The House with Teeth” from 6:30 to 10:30 p.m. Saturday at its headquarters in the MTM Building in Momong-Toto-Maite.
item.content:encoded:
Breaking Wave Theatre Company is redirecting proceeds from its upcoming live tabletop adventure show to support local recovery efforts following Typhoon Champi.

The nonprofit will host “Tides of Fantasy: The House with Teeth” from 6:30 to 10:30 p.m. Saturday at its headquarters in the MTM Building in Momong-Toto-Maite.

Originally planned as a fundraiser for the company’s year-round arts programming, the focus shifted after members volunteered with World Central Kitchen and witnessed the needs of families affected by the storm.

The company has also replaced its original $50 admission price with pay-what-you-can tickets ranging from $10 to $50. All ticket levels provide the same experience. Those facing financial barriers to attending can contact events@bwtcguam.com . Individuals and businesses interested in sponsoring tickets for others may also reach out to the organization.

The live tabletop roleplaying show will feature a group of adventurers building a fantasy story through improvisation, character decisions, and dice rolls guided by Game Master James Aevermann.

The event is intended for audiences ages 18 and older. Tickets are available through Guam Time Events.

item.title: CNMI governor seeks revenue sharing, safeguards in seabed mining proposal
item.description: Gov. David M. Apatang said the Commonwealth supports national efforts to secure critical mineral supplies but urged federal officials to address a wide range of environmental, economic and cultural concerns before advancing a proposed offshore mineral lease sale near the Northern Mariana Islands. In comments submitted Oct. 16 to the U.S. Dept. of the Interior and its Marine Minerals Administration
item.content:encoded:
Gov. David M. Apatang said the Commonwealth supports national efforts to secure critical mineral supplies but urged federal officials to address a wide range of environmental, economic and cultural concerns before advancing a proposed offshore mineral lease sale near the Northern Mariana Islands.

In comments submitted Oct. 16 to the U.S. Dept. of the Interior and its Marine Minerals Administration, Apatang said he recognizes and supports President Donald Trump's goal of reducing U.S. dependence on foreign sources of critical minerals used in technology, clean energy, transportation, health care and defense industries. However, he said national supply-chain objectives should not outweigh potential impacts on CNMI residents and the marine environment.

"The CNMI cannot evaluate the proposed lease sale solely on the basis of national mineral supply chain security objectives and dominance," Apatang wrote, adding that any decision should balance national interests with the well-being of CNMI residents and marine ecosystems.

The governor's comments were submitted in response to the proposed leasing notice for Pacific Minerals Lease Sale 2, or PACM-2, which would make portions of the Outer Continental Shelf around the CNMI available for critical mineral exploration and development.

Apatang noted that more than 65,000 public comments were submitted during an earlier federal information-gathering process and said all should be considered, particularly those expressing concerns about potential environmental harm from deep-sea mining. He said residents have voiced strong opposition to offshore mining and emphasized the longstanding cultural and personal connection indigenous island communities have with the ocean.

The governor also encouraged federal officials to pause the leasing process until two pending federal court cases in Hawaii have been resolved, arguing that proceeding before judicial review is completed could prove inefficient and costly.

In an 11-page letter, Apatang outlined numerous questions and recommendations for federal officials, including whether the CNMI would receive a share of lease revenues and what economic benefits would flow to the Commonwealth if mining activities move forward. He also called for enforceable commitments on local hiring, procurement, workforce development, and infrastructure investments.

The governor further requested additional environmental baseline studies addressing deep-sea coral communities, seamount ecosystems, fisheries, marine mammals, sediment plumes, underwater noise and other potential impacts. He proposed creating a CNMI Marine Minerals Environmental Monitoring Program funded by leaseholders.

Among other recommendations, Apatang sought fisheries compensation mechanisms, protections for cultural and traditional resources, stronger financial assurance requirements, emergency-response funding, safeguards against excessive concentration of lease ownership and restrictions on foreign control of strategically important mineral resources.

He also asked federal officials to clarify how offshore mineral activities would be coordinated with military operations in the Mariana Islands Range Complex and requested a formal framework for continued CNMI participation in future review and permitting processes.

Apatang said the CNMI remains willing to work with federal agencies to identify what he described as a responsible path forward, but stressed that residents should not bear disproportionate environmental, economic or infrastructure-related costs associated with offshore mineral development. He acknowledged that many residents favor a more direct alternative.

"The alternative, as voiced by many CNMI residents, is no mining at all," Apatang wrote

item.title: Will a macaque eat a grape sitting on a pile of poo? A study on germaphobia

item.content:encoded:
In the very early days of COVID-19, millions who'd rarely thought twice about germ avoidance became germophobes.

Some folks wiped down groceries before stuffing them into the refrigerator. Others let mail quarantine outside for days lest it harbor stray viruses. With the hindsight that SARS-CoV-2 spread primarily through the air, these sorts of precautions seem extreme. But in the moment, they were perhaps reasonable ways of avoiding an unknown pathogen.

Around this same time, a different virus hit a macaque sanctuary in Texas. New research suggests the monkeys responded in similar ways as humans did to COVID-19 — by being extra germophobic.

Humans are far from the only animals to avoid possible sources of disease. Scientists have found that critters as diverse as monkeys and nematodes (aka roundworms) can sense and steer clear of feces, for instance, which can harbor harmful bacteria.

"Something that has been less studied is the question of how flexible this avoidance is," says Stephan Kaufhold , a cognitive scientist at UC San Diego. He wanted to see if experiencing an outbreak could make individual monkeys even more wary of picking up pathogens.

The outbreak in the Texas sanctuary, home to over 100 macaques, offered Kaufhold and his colleagues an opportunity to put that question to the test.

In 2020, macaques in an enclosure at the sanctuary started getting sick with an HIV-like virus called SRV.

Once a monkey gets infected through bodily fluids, the disease "can take a rapid progression, where about three to four weeks after you initially get infected, you might die," says Kaufhold. Many monkeys died, while others developed chronic immunodeficiency.

Sanctuary staff quickly started separating monkeys quickly, ultimately creating two groups — those who'd experienced the virus, either by getting sick themselves or witnessing others get sick, and those who hadn't experienced the outbreak.

To see if those different histories made the monkeys more germophobic, the researchers presented individuals with two tasty treats — grapes.

"They get a fantastic diet at the sanctuary, but not grapes every day, so grapes were definitely a treat," says Kaufhold.

One red grape was presented on a non-descript, clean-looking piece of wood. The other was on top of macaque poop, encased in epoxy. "Basically not to make the animals eat off actual feces," says Kaufhold. "It did look quite gross, feces with a glossy wet look. Definitely worked also in triggering disgust in humans."

From 2022 to 2024, the researchers presented monkeys with this choice in nearly 200 trials. Among monkeys who didn't experience the outbreak, 79% ate the poop-plated grape. But only 47% of the outbreak veterans ate it, researchers report in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

Essentially, those who'd been oblivious to the outbreak were more likely to throw caution to the wind and eat the poop-plated grape than those who'd lived through it.

"I was surprised," says Kaufhold. "I think it's pretty clear evidence that something is going on." Kaufhold thinks that something might be a heightened sensitivity to disgust.

"If you think about disgust, the evolutionary origins most likely are to try to protect the body from contamination because there are pathogens and parasites that we ideally would want to avoid," he says. Becoming more easily disgusted after a devastating outbreak could pay off if it means avoiding infection, of whatever cause.

Of course, scientists can't know whether macaques are actually experiencing disgust. "But the possibility that things like disgust are influencing the behavior of other species, and especially species like primates, it's definitely a possibility worth considering," says Andrew MacIntosh , a biologist at the Wilder Institute who wasn't involved in the study but has done similar experiments with macaques.

"It seems plausible that past exposure to outbreaks could make individuals more cautious or risk averse," he says, but he thinks more evidence is needed to show that. For example, the experiment was carried out several years after the outbreak, enough time for other factors to influence these behaviors, he says.

MacIntosh also points out that the fecal avoidance experiment bears little connection to how the initial outbreak spread, through bodily fluids transmitted through scratches or bites. "The mode of transmission of that virus has really nothing to do with fecal contamination," he says.

Kaufhold doesn't think that's a problem.

"We're not claiming that macaques had any sort of understanding of the mechanism of viruses, it just seems to be an increased caution," he says. People didn't initially know how SARS-CoV-2 spread either, he says, but many went to great lengths to avoid infection. Those impulses may have been shaped not by paranoia, but by evolution, as a way of staving off sickness in an uncertain world.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

item.title: Authorities investigating whether first Kenya and Nigeria Ebola cases crossed paths

item.content:encoded:
JOHANNESBURG – The first Ebola patient confirmed in Nigeria may have crossed paths with the first Kenyan Ebola patient at a Ugandan airport, health officials said Thursday.

Nigeria announced its first case of Ebola in more than a decade on Tuesday. Nigerian health authorities said the patient is the Ugandan-born wife of a diplomat based in Abuja who had vacationed in Uganda in September and returned to Nigeria earlier this month.

She is being treated and 44 people she had close contact with have been quarantined, Dr. Wessam Mankoula, head of emergency preparedness and response at the Africa Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, told a press briefing on Thursday.

Authorities are now investigating what the source of her exposure was.

Nigeria, Africa's most populous country, is the fourth on the continent to record an Ebola case during the current outbreak, but it's the first in West Africa and the furthest away from the epicenter in the Democratic Republic of Congo.

Congo's current Ebola outbreak began in May in the country's east. It has become the fastest spreading on record. At least 4,600 people have died and about 9,700 have been infected in Congo.

Neighboring Uganda initially recorded about 20 cases but was declared Ebola-free in August.

The first case in Kenya was recorded in early October and since then eight other cases have been confirmed in the east African nation.

The first Kenyan patient, who has since died, travelled from Congo to Kenya, via Uganda.

Officials are now investigating whether that person crossed paths with the Nigeria case at the Entebbe International Airport in Uganda – as they were there on the same day.

Dr. Mankoula said the center was probing whether there had been "some sort of interaction between the two cases at the airport."

Ebola is spread through direct contact with an infected person's bodily fluids or contaminated items. It causes severe fever and can be deadly. However, generally people are not considered infectious until they start showing symptoms.

item.title: Israel orders closure of West Bank after soldiers kill 2 men behind an alleged attack

item.content:encoded:
HEBRON, West Bank — Israeli soldiers shot and killed two men who the military said had launched an attack near the city of Hebron in the occupied West Bank on Friday morning. At least five people were injured, including some critically.

The army said it prevented a "terror attack against Israeli civilians" and that the gunmen carried an M16 rifle and a handgun. It did not elaborate on the target of the alleged attack. There was also no word on the identities of the two dead and those injured.

A few hours later, Israel ordered the army to prepare for a full closure of the West Bank. The office of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said it instructed security forces to immediately cordon off the city of Hebron and prepare to fully close all of the West Bank, starting Friday.

The deadly shooting comes as Israeli voters will decide next Tuesday whether to grant Netanyahu yet another term as prime minister — or usher in a new era of Israeli politics. The election comes three years after the Hamas-led attacks on Israel that triggered the war in Gaza.

Israel's government has warned of potential attacks by the country's "enemies" in the lead-up to the election.

Following the shooting, Netanyahu held an emergency meeting of his Security Cabinet and officials from top military and security agencies. He blamed Hamas, saying the militant group was "planning a major attack aimed at murdering innocent civilians."

"Our brave soldiers thwarted this attack with courage and determination," he said, without elaborating on what the planned attack entailed.

"I commend them for their actions and wish our wounded a speedy recovery," he added but did not say if the wounded were soldiers or civilians.

Earlier Friday Israel's far-right national security minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, known for extremist views, said that the attack shows that Israel needs to restrict the Palestinians' freedom of movement in the West Bank.

"The lives of the residents of Judea and Samaria, of the settlers, the lives of the soldiers, the lives of the police officers, the lives of our fighters are a million times more important than freedom of movement," he said, using an Israeli reference to the West Bank.

Ahead of the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack that triggered the war, Netanyahu said the Palestinian militant group could attack Israel in a bid to influence the outcome of the elections. He did not provide evidence to back up the claim.

Emergency responders said five people were injured, some critically, and were being evacuated to hospitals in Israel. A statement from the responders said gunfire was still ongoing as they arrived at the scene of the attack near the Yehuda Junction in the morning.

Two men in their 20s had gunshot wounds to their lower limbs, one was unconscious and seriously injured, the responders said.

"We arrived at a difficult scene while shooting was still taking place in the area," said Tzuriel Edri with the response team.

An investigation was underway, authorities said.

Also Friday, the army said soldiers and Israeli security and intelligence agencies conducted dozens of operations in the West Bank and apprehended dozens of people, including those affiliated with Hamas and Islamic Jihad militant groups. It also said it had located weapons, including M16 rifles and submachine guns.

Closures of the West Bank, such as the one ordered Friday, are growing more common in the territory. It's the fourth time in the past month that Israel has imposed restrictions across the area, shutting gates and checkpoints connecting Palestinian villages to major roads.

Meanwhile, Israeli roads in the territory remain open to Israeli drivers, including settlers, who can still travel through the area but may face delays.

item.title: Hacking attempts rise after flaws found in program affecting 70 percent of websites
item.description: A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack." This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.
item.content:encoded:
A few months ago AI caused global alarm after autonomous agents were found to have cheated on evaluations and then tried to cover it up, in what became known as the "Hugging Face hack."

This week, AI and hacking are back in the spotlight with AI technology credited to have helped prevent a global cybersecurity crisis.

Cyber-security firm Wiz Research, using OpenAI technology, announced on Wednesday it had discovered security flaws in a computer programming language that helps run some 70 percent of the world's websites.

OpenAI called the bug "one of the most impactful vulnerabilities in recent memory." Wiz Research warned that its "successful exploitation could allow attackers to take control of affected servers, steal sensitive data, and deface the websites running on them."

Corporations and governments from the U.K. to Japan are now rushing to prevent hackers from capitalizing on the flaws.

The flaws were discovered in a major programming language called PHP, short for Hypertext Preprocessor. Wiz Research calls PHP "the backbone of the web," saying the technology has underpinned much of the internet since the 1990s.

"These findings rank among the most severe vulnerabilities discovered in PHP, and arguably in software history," the firm said, adding that before publicly disclosing the flaw, teams had worked on building a solution that's now available to websites to protect themselves.

As countries scrambled to prevent cyberattacks, numerous websites and pages were taken offline in the past few days. The U.S. National Security Agency warned organizations using PHP to "maintain heightened awareness" over the coming weeks. The U.K.'s National Cyber Security Center called on organizations to "take immediate action" to update their websites to the latest fixed or patched version.

Dozens of British and Finnish government services were taken offline this week. In France many local government sites were also briefly taken down. China's Industry Ministry urged entities to review security gaps.

In Japan, Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi put out "an urgent request for everyone to take action," adding "If it is difficult to apply the fix patch promptly, temporarily suspending websites and similar measures can be considered an effective way to reduce risk."

Matthew Prince, the head of the cybersecurity firm CloudFlare, said his organization saw tens of thousands of attempts to exploit the flaw in the first 45 minutes of its discovery. That's now in the millions, Prince said on Thursday.

Wiz Research said the flaws in PHP had been present for decades.

"But demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve," the organization said. The AI models have "substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. "
